Seminar Title:

Deciphering the role of marine filamentous fungal biofilm and mycelium based biocomposite for bioremediation of lead and phenanthrene co-pollutants

Seminar Type:

Defence Seminar

Department:

Life Science

Speaker Name:

Abhaya Dayini Behera ( Rollno : 520ls2003)

Speaker Type:

Student

Venue:

LS Seminar Room

Date and Time:

30 Oct 2026 02.30 pm

Contact:

Surajit Das

Abstract:

Marine filamentous fungi isolated from the coastal regions of Odisha were explored&nbspfor lead [Pb(II)] and phenanthrene removal potential. A total of 116 morphologically&nbspdistinct isolates were obtained from sediment, water, and leaf litter samples,&nbspcollected from Bhitarkanika mangroves, Chilika Lake and Paradip port. Among&nbspthese, six isolates exhibited biofilm-forming, Pb(II) and phenanthrene tolerating,&nbsp and lignolytic enzyme producing potential. Aspergillus terreus HLP5 demonstrated&nbsphighest Pb(II) and phenanthrene removal eficiency. Exposure to co-pollutants&nbsp(25-500 ppm, 1:1 ratio) altered biofilm maturation, mycelial aggregation, expression&nbspof biofilm and extracellular matrix (ECM)-associated genes, ECM composition and&nbspconformation. Reduced fluorescence intensity of tryptophan residues (290/355 nm)&nbspindicated binding interaction between ECM-protein and co-pollutants. ECM-rich&nbspbiofilm showed enhanced resilience to co-pollutant induced oxidative stress. A.&nbspterreus HLP5 biofilm achieved 75.57 &plusmn 3.02% phenanthrene and 98.45 &plusmn 0.04% Pb(II)&nbspremoval after 10 days of incubation under 50 ppm co-pollutant concentration.&nbspTranscriptomic analysis revealed 27006 transcripts of which 7871 were&nbspupregulated, 6688 were downregulated, and 12447 neutrally expressed between&nbspcontrol and treated samples. Upregulation of catA, AtEh1, and ShyA along with&nbspidentification of phenanthrene metabolites indicated its degradation through two&nbspdistinct pathways. Response surface methodology predicted ~87% of&nbspphenanthrene removal under optimized conditions. SEM-EDX confirmed Pb(II)&nbspbiosorption on mycelial surface. Mycelium based biocomposites fabricated from&nbspwheat bran, rice husk, and spent tea leavesexhibited lightweight, porous,&nbsphydrophobic, and biodegradable nature with thermal stability, mechanical strength&nbspand co-pollutant removal ability. These findings highlight fungal biofilm and&nbspmycelium based biocomposite as sustainable alternatives for remediation of co-pollutant contaminated environment.
